flashcards.q: What happens to a value when its owner goes out of scope?
flashcards.a: It is dropped deterministically at that point (Drop::drop runs), in reverse order of declaration -- no GC pause, no tracing, decided entirely at compile time.

flashcards.q: Why does assigning a String to another variable move it, but assigning an i32 copies it?
flashcards.a: String owns a heap allocation; a bit-copy would create two owners of the same allocation and a double-free when both drop. i32 is pure stack data with nothing to free, so bit-copying is trivially safe (the Copy trait).

flashcards.q: State the borrow rule in one sentence.
flashcards.a: At any point, either any number of shared &T references or exactly one exclusive &mut T reference to the same data -- never both at once.

flashcards.q: What bug class does the borrow rule make statically unrepresentable?
flashcards.a: Aliasing plus mutation -- e.g. holding a &T into a Vec while a &mut T reallocates its backing buffer (iterator invalidation / use-after-free), undefined behavior in C++ but a compile error in Rust.

flashcards.q: What did Non-Lexical Lifetimes (NLL, 2018 edition) change?
flashcards.a: A borrow's live range is now based on actual last USE (control-flow analysis) instead of ending at the enclosing lexical scope's closing brace -- accepts strictly more valid programs without weakening safety.

flashcards.q: Do lifetime annotations ('a) have a runtime cost?
flashcards.a: No -- they are a compile-time-only proof mechanism with zero runtime representation or cost. The proof replaces what a GC would otherwise check via runtime tracing.
The data is valid for the entire remaining execution of the program. String literals get this for free (embedded in the binary's read-only section).

flashcards.q: Why is a naive doubly-linked list hard to write in safe Rust?
flashcards.a: A prev back-pointer needs a reference tied to a node simultaneously owned one link further back -- the ownership model can't express that aliasing safely. Standard fixes: Rc<RefCell<Node>>, arena + usize indices, or unsafe raw pointers.

flashcards.q: How does ownership give compile-time data-race freedom across threads, not just within one thread?
flashcards.a: A data race is unsynchronized concurrent access with at least one write -- exactly what the borrow rule already forbids in a single thread. Extended across threads via the Send/Sync marker traits, giving compile-time data-race prevention safe Rust provides that GC'd languages don't.

flashcards.q: When is reaching for .clone() a legitimate answer versus a red flag?
flashcards.a: Legitimate when the function genuinely needs an owned, independent copy. A red flag when it's used reflexively to silence a borrow-checker error without understanding it -- a real, profilable O(n) allocation cost hiding an unresolved design question.
If there is exactly one input lifetime parameter, it is assigned to all elided output lifetimes.

flashcards.q: Why does fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str need an explicit lifetime annotation?
flashcards.a: With two input references, elision rule 2 (single input lifetime -> output) doesn't apply -- the compiler can't guess whether the output ties to x's or y's lifetime, so the programmer must state the constraint explicitly.
